head: Passkeys vs passwords explained: how they work on iPhone and Android
dek: A passkey lets you sign in with your face, fingerprint or phone PIN instead of a password, and because it never leaves your device as a secret you could type in, a fake website can't trick you into handing it over.

p: A passkey replaces the password for one account. When you make one, your device creates a pair of keys: the website keeps the public one, and the private one stays with you. Apple's page on passkey security says there is no shared secret, so there's nothing on the site's side that could leak and be reused.

You unlock it the way you unlock your phone. Google's help page says a passkey uses your fingerprint, face scan or screen lock, such as a PIN. Because it can't be written down, copied or shared, Google says it resists phishing: a fake login page gets nothing it can use.

On Apple devices, passkeys sync between your iPhone, iPad and Mac through iCloud Keychain, which Apple says is end-to-end encrypted with keys it doesn't know. An Apple Account needs two-factor authentication to use it. If you lose one device, the others still have your passkeys, and Apple says they can be recovered through iCloud Keychain even if you lose all of them, with your account password, a code sent by text and a device passcode.

On Android, Google says your phone may create passkeys for your Google Account for you, and that passkeys can also be stored in another password manager you use. Bitwarden, for example, said on 18 November 2026 that its desktop app now works as the passkey provider in Windows 11 and macOS, so the system's own passkey window can save passkeys to a Bitwarden vault; on Windows, the app has to come from the Microsoft Store.

sections.h: Using one on a computer that isn't yours
p: Your passkey stays on your phone, but you can still use it elsewhere. Google explains that on a computer's sign-in page you pick the passkey option, a QR code appears, you scan it with your phone, approve the sign-in and confirm with your face, fingerprint or PIN. Bluetooth needs to be on, because the phone has to be near the computer.

Google warns against creating a passkey on a shared device: anyone who can unlock that device can get into your account, even after you sign out. You can remove a passkey in your Google Account's security settings, and if a phone is lost or stolen, you can sign in on another device and remove that phone's passkey.

sections.h: How many people use them now
p: On 15 October 2026 the FIDO Alliance, the industry group behind the standard, published its Passkey Index with data from 15 consumer services, including Amazon, Google, Microsoft, PayPal, TikTok and WhatsApp. Across them, 36% of successful sign-ins used a passkey, up from 26% the year before, and passkey sign-ins worked 93% of the time against 78% for passwords and text-message codes. They were also about 2.8 times faster. FIDO estimates 7 billion passkeys are in use, though it doesn't say how it counted, and it notes the group of services changed between years.

In one week of August 2026, three research teams published attacks around passkeys on Windows and in Chrome's passkey sync. According to Start with Identity, none of them broke the passkey standard itself; all three needed malware or other code already running on the computer, and Microsoft fixed one of the problems in its July 2026 Windows updates.

Passkeys don't replace a password everywhere yet. Google lets you keep your password and switch back by turning off "Skip password when possible". Some school and work accounts may not allow passkey-only sign-in.

means: If you use passkeys, a fake login page or a leaked password list can't give away your sign-in; the risk moves to your phone and the account that syncs your passkeys, so those need a screen lock and two-factor sign-in.
todo: For your Google Account, create a passkey at myaccount.google.com under Passkeys and security keys and keep your phone's screen lock on. On iPhone, keep iCloud Keychain on and two-factor authentication set up. Make passkeys only on devices you alone use, keep your computer updated, and remove the passkey of a lost phone from another device.
